slides.title: The reaction history determines the next step
slides.section: The reaction history determines the next step
paragraphs: A 52-year-old with a susceptible bacterial infection has an amoxicillin allergy label. At age 8, a rash appeared several days into treatment. There were no mouth sores, blisters, breathing symptoms, or hospitalization. The patient has avoided penicillins since then.
What was the drug, when did the reaction start, what actually happened, was treatment required, and which beta-lactams have been tolerated since?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
The reaction history determines the next step A 52-year-old with a susceptible bacterial infection has an amoxicillin allergy label. At age 8, a rash appeared several days into treatment. There were no mouth sores, blisters, breathing symptoms, or hospitalization. The patient has avoided penicillins since then. What was the drug, when did the reaction start, what actually happened, was treatment required, and which beta-lactams have been tolerated since? Up to 10% of patients report a penicillin allergy, but fewer than 10% of those evaluated with testing have a current immediate IgE-mediated allergy. The discrepancy reflects inaccurate labels, rashes caused by the underlying infection, and loss of sensitization over time. The history still matters. A label of "rash" is not enough information. [1] [2] An inaccurate label often leads to broader or less effective therapy. That is associated with more adverse drug effects, C. difficile infection, resistant organisms, longer hospitalization, and higher cost. The goal is not to make the label disappear. The goal is to give the best antibiotic safely. [2]

slides.title: Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam
slides.section: Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam
rows: Usually within minutes to about 1 hour, but may occur within several hours
Clarify the culprit and timing. Use the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Classify the reaction before choosing another beta-lactam Timing and phenotype matter more than the word allergy. Pattern Typical timing Typical findings Resident implication Immediate, IgE-mediated Usually within minutes to about 1 hour, but may occur within several hours Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, anaphylaxis Clarify the culprit and timing. Use the local allergy pathway and review side-chain relationships before selecting therapy. Cytotoxic Days to weeks Immune hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia Do not use a routine challenge pathway. Avoid the culprit and obtain specialist guidance. Immune complex Days to weeks Serum sickness-like reaction, drug fever, or interstitial nephritis Skin testing for immediate allergy does not establish safety. Avoid the culprit and obtain guidance. Delayed, T-cell mediated Usually days to weeks Benign morbilliform eruption, or severe disease such as SJS/TEN, DRESS, or AGEP Separate a benign eruption from a severe cutaneous reaction. Never use PEN-FAST or routine challenge to clear a severe delayed reaction. Intolerance or nonallergic history Variable Isolated nausea, diarrhea, headache, family history, or a label without a patient reaction These findings alone do not establish immune-mediated allergy. Document the history accurately. The classic Gell-Coombs categories help organize the phenotype, but real reactions do not always fit neatly into one box. Ask specifically about mucosal injury, skin peeling, facial edema, eosinophilia, kidney or liver injury, cytopenias, treatment required, and subsequent beta-lactam tolerance. [1] [4]

slides.title: A penicillin allergy does not automatically exclude cefazolin
slides.section: A penicillin allergy does not automatically exclude cefazolin
paragraphs: Contemporary estimates place penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity at roughly 2%, far below the older 8-10% teaching. Most clinically important cross-reactivity follows R1 side-chain similarity rather than cephalosporin generation. [4]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
A penicillin allergy does not automatically exclude cefazolin Contemporary estimates place penicillin-cephalosporin cross-reactivity at roughly 2%, far below the older 8-10% teaching. Most clinically important cross-reactivity follows R1 side-chain similarity rather than cephalosporin generation. [4] For an unverified, nonanaphylactic penicillin allergy without a severe delayed phenotype, the 2022 practice parameter supports routine cephalosporin administration without preceding testing or added precautions. It also supports a structurally dissimilar cephalosporin such as cefazolin after penicillin anaphylaxis. This does not clear a cefazolin allergy or make cefazolin appropriate after a severe delayed beta-lactam reaction. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is very low; the same parameter supports carbapenem administration after penicillin or cephalosporin allergy, including anaphylaxis, without routine preceding testing or added precautions. [4] For the opening case, a remote benign rash may qualify for supervised direct amoxicillin challenge under the current pathway. If a cephalosporin is the appropriate treatment, the penicillin label alone need not delay its use. Choosing cefazolin and removing a penicillin label are separate decisions.

slides.title: Document what was tested and what the result means
slides.section: Document what was tested and what the result means
paragraphs: After a successful evaluation, update the allergy list as well as the note. Record the culprit history, drug and dose administered, date, observation period, and outcome. Document beta-lactams that were tolerated. Explain the result to the patient and communicate it to the next clinician. An uneventful immediate observation does not guarantee that no delayed rash will occur. [2] [4]

If the same patient instead recalls blistering and oral ulcers, stop. A remote severe reaction is still a severe reaction. Avoid the culprit and obtain specialist guidance rather than using a low PEN-FAST score or a routine test dose.

slides.title: Know what the validation studies did and did not establish
slides.section: Know what the validation studies did and did not establish
paragraphs: PEN-FAST is a clinical decision rule, not a complete allergy evaluation. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original derivation and validation cohorts. The PALACE randomized trial found that direct oral challenge was noninferior to skin testing followed by challenge in carefully selected adults with PEN-FAST below 3. Neither study supports bypassing phenotype review, challenging patients with severe delayed reactions, or performing an unmonitored dose. [5] [6]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Know what the validation studies did and did not establish PEN-FAST is a clinical decision rule, not a complete allergy evaluation. A score below 3 had a negative predictive value of 96.3% in the original derivation and validation cohorts. The PALACE randomized trial found that direct oral challenge was noninferior to skin testing followed by challenge in carefully selected adults with PEN-FAST below 3. Neither study supports bypassing phenotype review, challenging patients with severe delayed reactions, or performing an unmonitored dose. [5] [6] Side-chain charts are structural aids, not outcome calculators. Published charts disagree about some partial similarities. The most reliable high-yield pairings are amoxicillin with cefadroxil, ampicillin with cephalexin or cefaclor, and ceftazidime with aztreonam. Cefazolin has a unique R1 side chain. The reaction phenotype remains more important than a green cell on a chart. [4] [8] When the preferred drug is being withheld because of an allergy label, the consultant should state whether the concern is immediate allergy, severe delayed hypersensitivity, side-chain cross-reactivity, or simple uncertainty. That distinction determines whether the next step is routine administration, supervised challenge, skin testing, desensitization, or avoidance.
